purpose: Ways to make a well-worn trope feel new. A trope the case uses on purpose is declared in the bible (premise.tropes_embraced) with one of these lenses; declared tropes are exempt from the trope warning. Cliche phrasing stays banned regardless: the familiar thing lives in the structure, never in stock sentences. Abstract only: no story.
sources: Viktor Shklovsky, 'Art as Technique' (1917): defamiliarisation, making the familiar strange enough to be seen again.
Steve Neale, Genre (1980): genre pleasure as repetition with difference.
Umberto Eco, 'Casablanca: Cult Movies and Intertextual Collage' (1984): cliches used knowingly gain new force.
Project craft report, principle 6, 'The Double Bluff Re-imagined'; John Curran, Agatha Christie's Secret Notebooks (2009).
Mystery Engine Design Research, Track 3 (MASKS and REFRAMES) and Track 6 (archival humanity).

lenses.name: The trope is the default reading
lenses.move: Let the genre-savvy player recognise the trope early and believe it. It is the false lead or the cover story; the truth underneath is human-scale and reframes every document that seemed to confirm it.
lenses.risk: If the trope is simply false, the player feels cheated. Its trappings must have a true, human cause on paper.

lenses.name: Met only through procedure
lenses.move: The trope never appears directly. It is met through what the institution does about it: the forms, the quarantine checklist, the requisition, the incident numbering, the insurance query.
lenses.risk: Too dry. One person's paper must carry feeling.

lenses.name: Seen by someone looking elsewhere
lenses.move: Tell it through the person whose attention is on something ordinary: the cook's stock count, the radio operator's signal log, the contractor's invoice. The trope is the background to their own worry.
lenses.risk: The witness becomes a device. Their own want must matter on its own terms.

lenses.name: The aftermath the genre skips
lenses.move: The famous scene has already happened, or never quite does. The archive is the cleanup: the inquiry, the replacement order, the letter to a family, the shift rota with a name crossed out.
lenses.risk: Inertia. A question must still be live in the paperwork.

lenses.name: True, but beside the point
lenses.move: The uncanny thing is real within rules the archive teaches in plain terms, and it is not what the crime is about. The crime is a human act that used it, hid behind it, or was mistaken for it.
lenses.risk: Breaking fair play. Every rule the uncanny thing follows must be on paper before it matters.

lenses.name: The metaphor made literal
lenses.move: Take the trope's emotional meaning and make it a plain, checkable fact. A face you cannot trust becomes a borrowed credential; isolation becomes a logged communications blackout; the thing in the ice becomes a sample with a chain of custody.
lenses.risk: Too neat. Keep one thing unexplained that the case does not need.

lenses.name: The threat is the one being protected
lenses.move: The figure the trope casts as danger is the one someone is shielding, or the one doing the shielding.
lenses.risk: Sentimentality. Protection must have a cost on paper.

lenses.name: Cosmic stakes made personal
lenses.move: Whatever the trope threatens at scale, the case is about what it cost one ordinary person: a career, a promise, a friendship, a body that is wearing out.
lenses.risk: Losing the genre's charge. The large shadow stays in the background, felt but not explained.
